paragraphs: Column generation solves linear programs whose full collection of variables is too large to handle directly. It starts with a subset and adds variables over successive iterations. In vehicle routing, for example, a variable can represent a possible route, and there can be exponentially many routes. Choosing which variable to add influences how much work remains.

The paper introduces RLCG, which treats this choice as a sequential decision problem. Instead of selecting a column solely for its immediate appeal, a reinforcement learning policy accounts for its consequences for subsequent iterations. Graph neural networks represent the connections between variables and constraints, giving the policy a structured description of the optimization problem.

Experiments cover cutting stock and vehicle routing with time windows using the BPPLIB and Solomon benchmarks. Against a commonly used greedy policy, RLCG reduces column-generation iterations by an average of 22.4% and 40.9%, respectively, and converges faster. These results show that learning column-selection decisions can improve the efficiency of an established optimization procedure.
neurips-2022-a-deep-reinforcement-learni.tldr: RLCG learns column-selection decisions that account for later iterations, accelerating column generation on cutting-stock and vehicle-routing benchmarks.

paragraphs: Spectral clustering depends heavily on an affinity matrix, which records how similar data points are to one another. Building that matrix requires choosing a construction method and its settings. Those choices often depend on experience, and become especially difficult when clusters resemble one another or the dataset is large.

The paper automates selection by comparing candidate matrices produced by different methods and hyperparameters. It introduces a reliability measure called the relative-eigen-gap, derived from the graph Laplacian associated with each matrix. Grid search or Bayesian optimization then searches for a candidate with a favorable score. This supplies a common criterion for choices that would otherwise require separate manual judgments.

The authors also introduce an affinity-construction method using least-squares representation and thresholding, with theoretical support for its effectiveness. A large-scale extension has time complexity linear in the number of data points. Natural-image clustering experiments report greater versatility, accuracy, and efficiency than the evaluated baselines, supporting both the automated selection strategy and its practical scalability.
neurips-2022-a-simple-approach-to-automa.tldr: The method automates spectral-clustering choices by scoring candidate affinity matrices and adds an efficient construction method and large-scale extension.

paragraphs: Antibodies bind to particular antigens, with much of that binding determined by regions called complementarity-determining regions, or CDRs. Designing these regions involves both their amino-acid sequences and their three-dimensional structures. The paper develops a generative model that addresses these two connected aspects together while explicitly targeting a specified antigen structure.

The approach combines diffusion probabilistic models with equivariant neural networks to model CDR sequences and structures jointly. Its design supports several tasks within the same framework: generating a sequence and structure together, choosing a sequence for an existing backbone structure, and optimizing an antibody. This flexibility matters because antibody design can start from different amounts of existing structural information.

The authors evaluate the quality of generated sequences and structures across extensive experiments. They report that the model can achieve competitive binding-affinity results as measured by biophysical energy functions, alongside other protein-design metrics. These findings support the approach as a computational design method; the stated affinity evidence specifically comes from those energy-based measurements.
neurips-2022-antigen-specific-antibody-d.tldr: A diffusion-based model jointly designs antibody sequences and structures for specified antigens, with competitive results on computational protein-design measures.

paragraphs: An interactive private mechanism holds a dataset and answers queries that can depend on previous answers. Differential privacy limits what this interaction can reveal about an individual's participation. The paper asks how privacy guarantees combine when an adversary can interact with several independently running mechanisms and freely alternate queries among them.

This concurrent setting allows information obtained from one mechanism to shape questions sent to another. The authors prove optimal composition results for approximate differential privacy, Rényi differential privacy, and zero-concentrated differential privacy. Their theorems extend earlier work that established an optimal concurrent composition result for pure differential privacy.

The central conclusion is that interleaving queries gives the adversary no additional advantage in the studied composition setting. Consequently, accounting for the combined privacy cost does not require an extra penalty simply because these independent mechanisms support interactivity. The abstract also identifies concurrent independent work on another privacy framework that implies the approximate-privacy case, while this paper establishes results across the other named notions.
neurips-2022-composition-theorems-for-in.tldr: Optimal composition theorems show that interleaving queries to independently running private mechanisms adds no privacy cost under several major privacy notions.

paragraphs: Dataset distillation seeks a small synthetic training set that retains much of a larger dataset's useful information. One formulation repeatedly trains a model on the synthetic data, then adjusts that data based on the model's performance. Computing how changes to the data affect the entire training process can demand substantial memory and computation.

The paper introduces neural Feature Regression with Pooling, or FRePo, to address that bottleneck. Its optimization is analogous to truncated backpropagation through time, reducing the burden associated with differentiating through training. It also uses a pool of models to alleviate different forms of overfitting during distillation. Together, these choices aim to make synthetic datasets both cheaper to learn and more effective.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance with an order of magnitude less memory and two orders of magnitude faster training than previous methods. FRePo substantially improves results on CIFAR100, Tiny ImageNet, and ImageNet-1K. The paper also demonstrates benefits of high-quality distilled data for continual learning and membership-inference defense, extending its value beyond dataset compression alone.
neurips-2022-dataset-distillation-using-.tldr: FRePo learns effective synthetic datasets with substantially lower training and memory costs, while improving distillation and downstream applications.

paragraphs: Training data from untrusted sources can contain poisoned examples that implant a backdoor in a model. The paper starts from an observation about an already backdoored network: triggered examples have internal feature representations that change more under transformations than those of clean examples. That difference offers a way to distinguish suspicious training samples.

The authors turn the observation into a metric called feature consistency towards transformations, or FCT. A sample-distinguishing module uses this metric to separate likely poisoned and clean data. The paper then builds two defenses around that shared component, allowing the same signal to support different starting situations.

The first defense trains a model from scratch through a two-stage secure-training procedure. The second repairs an existing backdoored model by alternating between unlearning identified poisoned samples and relearning identified clean samples. Experiments on three benchmark datasets and eight attack types report better defense performance than state-of-the-art alternatives. The results support transformation sensitivity as a useful empirical signal for both training and repair.
neurips-2022-effective-backdoor-defense-.tldr: Feature sensitivity to transformations helps identify poisoned examples and supports defenses for both fresh training and backdoor removal.

paragraphs: Unsupervised outlier detection presents a difficult selection problem: practitioners must choose a detector and its hyperparameters without the usual labeled evidence for tuning. Deep detectors can introduce many such choices. The paper investigates how much these settings matter through a large-scale analysis involving more than 35,000 trained models.

The analysis finds substantial sensitivity, motivating ROBOD, an ensemble that combines models with different hyperparameter configurations. Combining configurations reduces reliance on selecting one particularly successful setting. To make this approach practical, ROBOD shares parameters, trains models in batches or simultaneously, and subsamples data. These strategies reduce the number of separately trained models and parameters required.

Experiments on image and tabular datasets report robust, state-of-the-art detection performance relative to the evaluated modern methods. ROBOD requires only 2–10% of the training time of a naïve hyper-ensemble whose members are trained independently. The contribution therefore addresses both sides of the selection problem: sensitivity to settings and the computational expense of covering multiple settings.
neurips-2022-hyperparameter-sensitivity-.tldr: ROBOD combines different hyperparameter configurations efficiently to deliver robust deep outlier detection without relying on a single configuration.

paragraphs: A model can fit its training data perfectly while capturing both meaningful structure and accidental noise. This paper studies that distinction through information: relevant bits help characterize the unknown process generating the data, while residual bits encode training noise. It uses residual information to quantify overfitting rather than relying solely on training loss.

The authors formulate an information-efficiency objective that favors relevant information while limiting residual information. They solve this optimization for a linear-regression problem, obtaining the information content of optimal algorithms. They then compare randomized ridge regression against that reference, assessing how efficiently it preserves useful information relative to the optimum.

The results characterize a fundamental trade-off between retaining signal and encoding noise. Using random matrix theory, the paper also studies the information complexity of learning a linear map in high dimensions and identifies information-theoretic counterparts of double and multiple descent. The work provides a precise analysis within linear regression, using that setting to clarify how fitting data and learning useful structure can differ.
neurips-2022-information-bottleneck-theo.tldr: An information-theoretic analysis of linear regression quantifies the trade-off between learning useful structure and retaining training noise.

paragraphs: When several objectives compete, optimization seeks a collection of useful compromises rather than one choice that wins on every measure. Finding those compromises becomes harder when evaluations are noisy and only a limited number are available. Multi-objective Bayesian optimization addresses this situation by choosing evaluations carefully to make effective use of the available budget.

The paper introduces Joint Entropy Search, or JES, as a rule for deciding what to evaluate next. It measures the joint information an evaluation can provide about the optimal inputs and their corresponding objective values. Considering these together connects uncertainty about which decisions are best with uncertainty about the outcomes those decisions achieve.

The authors develop several analytical approximations to make the acquisition function usable and extend it to selecting batches of evaluations. Tests on synthetic and real-world problems demonstrate effectiveness using hypervolume and weighted variants, measures for assessing sets of trade-offs. The contribution is an information-based selection strategy that treats the locations and outcomes of optimal compromises jointly.
neurips-2022-joint-entropy-search-for-mu.tldr: Joint Entropy Search selects evaluations by their combined information about optimal decisions and outcomes in multi-objective optimization.

paragraphs: A single-index model reduces a potentially high-dimensional input to one projection, then applies an unknown one-variable function to that projection. Both the relevant direction and the function must be learned. This captures situations where many measured variables conceal a much simpler predictive structure, making adaptation to that structure valuable.

Existing statistical understanding includes methods tailored specifically to single-index models. The paper instead studies whether a natural class of shallow neural networks can learn them through gradient flow. A defining feature of the analyzed networks is that neuron biases remain fixed at their random initial values. The result therefore concerns a particular network and training setup.

The authors show that this setup has a benign optimization landscape and derive generalization guarantees from that property. The guarantees match the near-optimal sample complexity of dedicated semi-parametric methods. This connects the behavior of neural-network training to statistical efficiency: in the studied setting, a shallow network can exploit the hidden one-dimensional structure with comparable data requirements.
neurips-2022-learning-single-index-model.tldr: Shallow networks with randomly fixed biases can learn single-index models through gradient flow with near-optimal sample-complexity guarantees.

paragraphs: Sequence variational autoencoders aim to represent sequences through a latent space that can support generation and manipulation. Training can fail to make meaningful use of that space because an autoregressive decoder may explain the sequence from its other inputs. This problem, called posterior collapse, undermines the purpose of learning a latent representation.

A common response is to randomly drop parts of the decoder input, reducing the information available through that route. The paper gives a theoretical account in terms of pointwise mutual information: dropout removes information supplied by the decoder input, which is compensated for through use of the latent space. This explanation motivates choosing dropout according to information rather than uniformly.

The authors propose an adversarial training strategy that learns information-based stochastic dropout. On standard text benchmarks, the targeted method improves sequence-modeling performance and increases information captured in the latent space compared with uniform dropout. The findings support making the dropout policy itself a learned component of sequence-VAE training.
neurips-2022-learning-to-drop-out-an-adv.tldr: Learning targeted dropout through adversarial training improves sequence modeling and latent-space information compared with uniform dropout.

paragraphs: Real-world time series can change their statistical behavior over time, making forecasting difficult. Normalizing a series can improve predictability, but it can also remove information needed to anticipate bursts and other changing behavior. The paper calls this over-stationarization and connects it to Transformers producing insufficiently distinct attention patterns for different series.

The proposed framework combines two interdependent modules. Series Stationarization standardizes input statistics and restores the corresponding statistics at the output. De-stationary Attention brings information about the original changing behavior back into the model's temporal dependencies. It does so by approximating distinguishable attention patterns associated with the raw series, aiming to retain useful information lost through normalization.

The authors report improvements across mainstream Transformer models, with mean squared error reductions of 49.43% for Transformer, 47.34% for Informer, and 46.89% for Reformer. These empirical results support treating normalization and attention jointly. The approach addresses both the difficulty of modeling changing distributions and the loss of predictive detail caused by making inputs statistically uniform.
neurips-2022-non-stationary-transformers.tldr: Non-stationary Transformers combine input normalization with attention that restores changing-series information, substantially improving reported forecasting errors.

paragraphs: A voting classifier combines predictions from a finite collection of classifiers into one decision. The paper asks how well that combined decision should perform beyond its training examples. Its analysis focuses on margins, which describe how strongly a vote favors a classification, providing more information than whether the final prediction is simply correct.

The authors use PAC-Bayes theory to prove margin-based generalization bounds. Their central construction draws on Dirichlet posterior distributions previously studied for training voting classifiers. The key distinction is that margins allow the resulting bounds to apply to non-randomized votes. This connects a probabilistic analytical framework to classifiers that make a fixed voting decision.

Across a number of classification tasks, the bounds provide state-of-the-art guarantees. These findings concern the strength of generalization guarantees for ensembles, rather than a reported universal improvement in prediction accuracy. They also contribute to the debate over margin-based explanations of ensemble generalization by showing how margins can support strong guarantees for finite, non-randomized voting classifiers.
neurips-2022-on-margins-and-generalisati.tldr: Margin-based PAC-Bayes bounds provide strong generalization guarantees for finite ensembles that use non-randomized voting.

paragraphs: Larger neural networks are often empirically more resistant to adversarial perturbations, but increasing size can also increase computation. Sparse mixture-of-experts models offer a way to add parameters while keeping computational cost roughly constant. The paper investigates whether this separation can provide robustness benefits without the corresponding expense of a larger dense model.

The theoretical analysis studies Lipschitz constants, which characterize how much a function can change as its input changes. Under particular conditions on routing and data structure, the authors show that mixtures of experts can have substantially smaller constants than dense counterparts. They also identify a vulnerability: robustness can deteriorate when the highest-weighted experts for an input implement sufficiently different functions.

ImageNet experiments with adversarial attacks find the evaluated mixtures more robust than dense models at the same computational cost. Additional observations show robustness to the choice of experts and indicate redundancy among experts in trained models. Together, the results connect conditional theoretical advantages with empirical evidence, while highlighting the importance of expert behavior and routing.
neurips-2022-on-the-adversarial-robustne.tldr: Sparse mixtures of experts show conditional theoretical and empirical robustness advantages over dense networks with comparable computational cost.

paragraphs: The paper makes one connection between interpretability and safety quantitative: how far can a model's behavior depart from a reference model regarded as safe? It formulates this as an optimization problem called maximum deviation. The resulting assessment is explicitly relative to the chosen reference, giving a concrete target for examining model behavior.

For decision trees and generalized linear and additive models, the authors show that maximum deviation can be computed exactly and efficiently. For tree ensembles, discrete optimization can still produce informative bounds. These results distinguish cases where the largest departure can be found precisely from cases where it can be bounded usefully.

The analysis extends to a broader class of piecewise Lipschitz functions using ideas from multi-armed bandits. Within that setting, interpretability yields tighter regret bounds for estimating maximum deviation. Case studies, including mortgage approval, illustrate the method and the insights obtained by searching for extreme departures. The contribution makes interpretability useful for a specific safety-assessment task rather than treating comprehensibility alone as a safety guarantee.
neurips-2022-on-the-safety-of-interpreta.tldr: Maximum deviation quantifies departures from a reference model regarded as safe, with interpretability enabling exact computations or tighter bounds.

paragraphs: Spatial precipitation downscaling seeks detailed rainfall maps from lower-resolution observations. Progress depends on having suitable paired data for training and evaluation. RainNet addresses this need with more than 62,400 low- and high-resolution map pairs covering over 17 years, providing a large organized resource for developing downscaling methods.

The maps include varied weather phenomena, such as hurricanes and squalls, and are arranged as image sequences with hourly maps. This organization exposes challenges associated with time and physical behavior, including temporal misalignment, temporal sparsity, and fluid properties. The dataset therefore supports studying precipitation as an evolving process rather than only as separate images.

The paper introduces two evaluation metrics and compares 14 models spanning deep-learning and traditional approaches. It also proposes an implicit physical estimation benchmark framework intended to learn the dataset's relevant characteristics. Extensive experiments demonstrate RainNet's value for training and evaluating downscaling models. Its contribution combines data, evaluation tools, and a modeling framework around the specific demands of precipitation reconstruction.
neurips-2022-rainnet-a-large-scale-image.tldr: RainNet provides paired precipitation maps, evaluation metrics, and benchmarks for learning to reconstruct rainfall at higher spatial resolution.

paragraphs: Reverse-engineering a backdoor trigger can help identify and repair a compromised neural network. Existing approaches considered in this paper constrain the trigger in the input, for example by limiting its size. That assumption misses triggers expressed through feature changes, such as image-style transformations, that do not take the form of a fixed input pattern.

The authors observe that both input-space and feature-space Trojans are associated with hyperplanes in the model's feature space. They use this shared structure to constrain trigger reconstruction. Moving the constraint into the representation space allows the method to address both kinds of backdoor within one reverse-engineering approach.

Experiments cover four datasets and seven attacks, comparing model detection and mitigation with existing defenses. The method reports average detection accuracy of 93%. For mitigation, it reduces attack success rate to 0.26% while leaving benign accuracy nearly unchanged. These reported results support the usefulness of feature-space constraints for detecting and mitigating the evaluated attacks, including those that violate a static-pattern assumption.
neurips-2022-rethinking-the-reverse-engi.tldr: Feature-space constraints enable reverse-engineering and mitigation of both static input triggers and feature-based Trojan attacks.

paragraphs: An autonomous system's perception module converts sensor measurements into estimates that a controller uses to act. A perception error matters for safety through the decisions it causes downstream. This paper designs perception around those consequences, evaluating errors in the context of the complete system operating in a closed loop.

The authors formulate a risk function that quantifies how a particular perceptual error affects overall safety. They use that function in two ways: adding a risk-dependent term to the training loss and generating training data in regions where risk is important. Both mechanisms direct learning toward errors and situations with greater safety consequences.

The approach is evaluated in a realistic aircraft detect-and-avoid application using vision. The reported design reduces collision risk by 37% relative to a baseline system. This demonstrates an application-specific benefit from connecting perception training to controller outcomes. The central contribution is a method for bringing system-level safety consequences into both the learning objective and the choice of training data.
neurips-2022-risk-driven-design-of-perce.tldr: Training perception around downstream safety risk reduces collision risk by 37% in the evaluated vision-based aircraft application.

paragraphs: Neural-network dynamic models repeatedly make noisy predictions to describe how a system evolves over time. Assessing their safety requires reasoning about distributions of possible trajectories. The paper develops stochastic barrier functions that provide lower bounds on the probability that a modeled system remains safe.

The authors construct these functions through convex optimization. Piecewise linear bounds on the neural network make it possible to formulate barrier synthesis as a sum-of-squares optimization problem. If the resulting lower bound exceeds a desired safety threshold, the system is certified. This gives a sufficient certification test based on a computable bound.

When that threshold is not met, the method generates controls intended to reduce unsafety robustly while intervening minimally. Convexity of the barrier function allows this control problem to be expressed as a linear program. Experiments demonstrate applicability to multidimensional models with multiple layers and hundreds of neurons per layer, and show that the controller can substantially improve safety probability.
neurips-2022-safety-guarantees-for-neura.tldr: Stochastic barrier functions provide safety-probability bounds for neural dynamic models and support controls that improve those probabilities.

paragraphs: Online allocation problems must make feasible choices as opportunities arrive, often under combinatorial constraints. A common approach first solves a relaxed problem that permits fractional choices, then rounds that solution into actual selections. Online contention resolution studies this rounding step when an adversary controls the order in which choices must be processed.

The paper focuses on greedy schemes against an almighty adversary, a particularly demanding setting. Intuitively, these schemes commit their decisions before the online process begins. The authors construct simple schemes with a 1/e selectability guarantee for single-item constraints, partition matroids, and transversal matroids, improving the previous 1/4 guarantee for these constraint families.

They also prove that no better competitive ratio than 1/e is possible in the studied setting. The construction and matching upper limit together establish optimality for these greedy schemes. This matters because it combines an implementation-oriented form of algorithm with the strongest achievable guarantee under the specified adversarial model, for constraints relevant to online combinatorial allocation.
neurips-2022-simple-and-optimal-greedy-o.tldr: Simple greedy online contention-resolution schemes achieve the optimal 1/e guarantee for three constraint families against an almighty adversary.

paragraphs: Delta tuning adapts a large pretrained model by optimizing only a small portion of parameters. Its effectiveness depends partly on where the trainable modules are placed, a choice commonly made by hand. The paper investigates whether automatically searching those placements can make better use of a restricted trainable-parameter budget.

S³Delta unifies several delta-tuning methods within a differentiable structure-search framework. It uses bi-level optimization to search the structure and a shifted global sigmoid method to explicitly control how many parameters are trainable. The search therefore addresses both the arrangement of adaptation modules and the size of the adaptation budget.

Experiments report that searched structures outperform manually designed and random structures while using fewer trainable parameters. With 0.01% trainable parameters, they retain more than 99% of fine-tuning performance. The reported advantage grows at budgets between 0.0009% and 0.01%. The structures are also transferable and explainable, suggesting that the search can inform later module design as well as produce efficient adaptations.
neurips-2022-sparse-structure-search-for.tldr: S³Delta automatically searches adaptation-module structures, retaining over 99% of reported fine-tuning performance with 0.01% trainable parameters.

paragraphs: Inverse problems work backward from observations to the quantities or relationships that produced them. The paper studies linear statistical inverse problems, where this recovery must account for the statistical nature of the data. It shows how stochastic gradient descent can be used as a solution method, linking inverse-problem estimation with a familiar learning algorithm.

The theoretical contribution includes consistency results and finite-sample bounds on excess risk. Consistency addresses the behavior of the estimator as data accumulate, while finite-sample bounds describe its error with a limited amount of data. The authors also modify stochastic gradient descent by using machine-learning methods to smooth its stochastic gradients, improving empirical performance.

The method is illustrated through functional linear regression, where the regression setup involves functional data. The examples include synthetic data and a classification task that predicts the main activity of bitcoin addresses from their balances. Together, the theory and examples connect a statistical guarantee for the basic approach with a practical gradient-smoothing modification and concrete applications.
neurips-2022-statistical-learning-and-in.tldr: The paper establishes statistical guarantees for stochastic-gradient solutions to linear inverse problems and improves empirical performance through gradient smoothing.

paragraphs: Distributed learning can spend substantial resources communicating updates between computing nodes. Compression reduces that traffic, but its design can benefit from information about the local optimization problem. Earlier smoothness-aware methods used matrices derived from local data to guide sparsification, with their analysis depending on the compression operator being linear.

This paper extends the strategy to arbitrary unbiased compression operators, making it applicable to stochastic quantization as well as sparsification. Its theoretical results guarantee communication-complexity savings over standard quantization. In particular, using n quantization blocks rather than one yields a theoretical reduction by an O(n) factor, where n is the number of nodes.

Numerical experiments on convex optimization problems compare the proposed methods with existing quantization schemes and smoothness-aware sparsification. The reported improvements cover iteration counts, total transmitted bits, and elapsed time. These findings connect the broader theoretical framework to measured efficiency: using local smoothness information can improve how updates are quantized and how quickly the distributed optimization proceeds.
neurips-2022-theoretically-better-and-nu.tldr: Smoothness-aware compression extends to unbiased quantization, yielding theoretical communication savings and faster reported convex optimization.

paragraphs: TVLT investigates whether useful visual-linguistic representations can be learned directly from images, video, and audio without first converting language into text. It uses homogeneous Transformer blocks with minimal design specific to each modality. The architecture omits text-oriented components such as tokenization and automatic speech recognition.

Training combines two objectives. Masked autoencoding asks the model to reconstruct missing patches of video frames and audio spectrograms, encouraging representations of each signal's content. Contrastive modeling aligns video and audio, connecting information across the two modalities. These objectives provide a route to learning shared representations directly from low-level audiovisual signals.

The paper reports performance comparable to a text-based counterpart on visual question answering, image retrieval, video retrieval, and multimodal sentiment analysis. It also reports 28-fold faster inference and one-third as many parameters. These results suggest that compact, efficient visual-linguistic representations can be learned without assuming an existing text representation, with the evidence grounded in the evaluated tasks and comparison.
neurips-2022-tvlt-textless-vision-langua.tldr: TVLT learns from raw visual and audio inputs, matching its text-based counterpart on evaluated tasks with faster inference and fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Recognizing a new concept can involve combining familiar parts and relationships rather than learning from examples of the whole. ZeroC aims to give machines this ability at inference time. It supports both recognizing concepts from symbolic descriptions and acquiring new concepts whose structure can then be communicated and reused.

The architecture represents a concept as a graph: nodes correspond to constituent concept models, and edges encode relationships. Energy-based models represent both concepts and relations, enabling composition during inference. A one-to-one mapping connects each symbolic graph to its corresponding energy-based model, linking an explicit description of a concept with a model usable for recognition.

The paper introduces learning and inference algorithms and demonstrates ZeroC on a challenging grid-world dataset designed to test zero-shot recognition and acquisition. The architecture supports applying communicated structures to classification and detection, including across domains. The contribution is a concrete mechanism for assembling and sharing new concepts from learned components, with its demonstrated capability evaluated in the stated grid-world setting.
neurips-2022-zeroc-a-neuro-symbolic-mode.tldr: ZeroC composes learned concepts and relations into symbolic graphs and energy-based models to recognize and acquire new concepts at inference time.
